opus-5.5.text:
I think what I've come to appreciate most is how much they changed the *interface* to the robot. For a long time, if you wanted a robot to do something new, you had to define the task very precisely: a reward function, a state representation, a specific pipeline for perception, planning, and control. Every new task was almost a new engineering project.

With vision-language-action models, you're borrowing a huge amount of prior knowledge from internet-scale vision and language pretraining. The robot already has some notion of what a "cup" is, what "put it next to the sink" means, what a cluttered kitchen looks like. You're not teaching it the world from scratch; you're mostly teaching it how to connect that understanding to motor commands. That's a big shift.

The second thing is the generalization you get almost for free. You train on a set of demonstrations, and then the model handles slightly different objects, different lighting, a different phrasing of the instruction. Not perfectly, but much better than the older, narrowly trained policies. That robustness to small variations matters a lot in real homes and factories, where nothing is ever exactly the same twice.

That said, I've also come to appreciate their limits. A VLA is very good at "what" and somewhat good at "where," but the "how," meaning the fine-grained, contact-rich, high-frequency part of manipulation, is still hard. Language and images are low-bandwidth relative to the physics of, say, inserting a plug or folding cloth. So a lot of the interesting work now is in the action side: better action representations, higher control frequencies, incorporating force and touch, and getting much more diverse robot data. Data is really the bottleneck. We have the internet for language, but we don't have an internet for robot actions yet.

So my honest view is that VLAs gave us a very good foundation, a kind of common sense layer for robots, but the last mile, making them reliable enough that you'd trust them for hours without supervision, is where the real challenge is now.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what I've come to appreciate most is that VLA models changed what the bottleneck is. For a long time in robotics, the hard part was perception and the hard part was planning, and you'd stitch together these brittle pipelines where each module had its own failure modes. A VLA model collapses that. You give it an image, you give it a language instruction, and it outputs actions directly. The thing I underestimated early on was how much the language side actually matters. It's not just a convenient interface for humans. Language gives the model a kind of compositional structure that lets it generalize to objects and situations it never saw during training, because the vision-language backbone already carries so much world knowledge from pretraining on internet data.

The second thing is humility about data. Everyone says "data is the bottleneck," but with VLA models you really feel it. A model can be enormous and well-pretrained, and still fall apart because you only have a few hundred demonstrations of a particular manipulation skill, collected in one lab, with one lighting condition. So I've come to appreciate that the architecture is almost the easy part now. The real craft is in how you collect, curate, and mix robot data with non-robot data, and how you decide what counts as a good demonstration in the first place.

And honestly, the third thing is that they fail in interesting ways. A classical controller fails predictably. A VLA model will do ninety percent of a task beautifully and then confidently grasp thin air. That failure mode taught me a lot about where the model's grounding is actually weak, and it's pushed the field toward thinking seriously about action tokenization, about closing the loop faster, about using the model's own uncertainty. So I'd say I appreciate them as much for what they reveal about the problem as for what they solve.

astra-6.text:
What I’ve come to appreciate is that vision-language-action models bring perception, instructions, and behavior into a shared framework. The robot has to connect what you say with what it sees, and then turn that into an action. That connection is really compelling because it offers a way to reuse knowledge across tasks instead of building every behavior separately.

But I also appreciate how much the physical world demands of these models. Understanding “pick up the cup” is one thing; grasping it reliably, noticing when it slips, and recovering is another. So for me, the exciting question is how broadly these models can generalize while still being dependable in those small, messy moments that make robotics hard.

sol-6.1.text:
What I’ve come to appreciate is that vision-language-action models give robots a way to connect what they see, what we ask them to do, and how they move. Those are often treated as separate problems, but in practice they’re deeply connected.

If I say, “Move that cup out of the way,” the robot has to figure out which cup I mean, what “out of the way” means in that setting, and how to move it. A VLA model offers a way to learn those connections together.

The exciting part is the possibility of transferring experience across tasks. But producing a plausible action is only the beginning. The robot also needs to recognize when something went wrong and recover. That’s where I think a lot of the real work is.
